sm: The Tuesday, November seventeenth edition opens with the news. President Trump is expected to land in the Philippines to begin an Asia trip, with talks planned on trade, nuclear weapons, Iran and Ukraine, then meetings in Beijing with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. The administration is also tightening limits on China's access to American AI computing power. On Friday's nationwide ground stop, the FAA says aging equipment was overwhelmed with data while a contractor replaced copper wiring with fiber optic lines. Vice President Vance says some equipment is fifty years old, and the administration wants fifty billion dollars from Congress. Also covered are a Chase software glitch, a third American carrier arriving near Iran, and a second trial for Lindsay Clancy starting March twenty-ninth. The FAA segment then begins.

Transportation analyst Mark Scribner of the Reason Foundation joins Nick Eichler to discuss the ground stop. Scribner was in the air when it began and spent two hours on the tarmac. He says the problem hit high-altitude and terminal control centers, and that safety was never really threatened. He argues the incident shows how outdated the system is, and that the FAA should have had redundancy and better oversight of its contractor. He says the current approach of throwing a one-time cash infusion at the legacy system is wrong. Instead, air traffic control should be in a state of constant modernization. The show then turns to Samuel Sey, a conservative Christian commentator deported to Canada, with his friend Aaron Baer, who says Sey believed his papers were in order.

Aaron Baer says Sey presented his documents at airport security and was detained, which shows he thought he was in the country legally. Something was wrong with the paperwork, and Sey accepts the consequences. Baer says Sey still supports immigration enforcement, because law and order is part of what makes America special. Sey's wife, Annie, and their three children have been helped by their church community. Baer sees no tension between enforcing the law and treating people justly. He says Sey is safe with his family in Canada, and they are working on how to bring him back. The program then reports on Anthropic's planned public stock offering, expected to raise up to sixty-five billion dollars. It follows Ailsa Woods, a marketing writer who lost a job to ChatGPT. Anthropic's models range from modest to extreme, and in the extreme case about fourteen million knowledge workers could lose jobs.

The AI report continues. Anthropic says the economy could grow up to fifteen percent a year in its most dramatic scenario, but only if companies adopt AI quickly, which is costly. Its models show wages rising, especially for people who work with their hands. Entry-level jobs could be harder to find. Woods believes people will prefer human-made content, and surveys show more than half of Americans think AI's risks outweigh its benefits. A lighter story follows about a gas price war in Powder Springs, Georgia, where prices fell below two dollars a gallon and police had to direct traffic. Then a story begins about Jane Schlenker, who wanted to join the military from a young age. She started writing to recruiters at twelve and enlisted in the Air Force in December 1973, after the draft ended.

Schlenker describes basic training with separate flights for women and men, a makeup class, and no women's barracks. She says early on it was an old boys club, and women had to do their jobs a little better than everyone else. She became the first woman to reach Chief Master Sergeant in the 442nd Fighter Wing and retired in 2002 after twenty-five years. She says she has no regrets. Then commentator Janie B. Cheney addresses Republican efforts to find silver linings after the midterm losses. She says expecting Democrats to fail is a rickety basis for hope. She points to the disciples on the Friday of Jesus's crucifixion as the biggest disappointment, and says Jesus promised their sorrow would turn to joy. Tomorrow's show features Hunter Baker.
